title: Load Balancing & Proxies
summary: One machine can't serve the internet. A load balancer is the traffic cop that spreads requests across many servers, hides them behind one address, and quietly drops the dead ones.

blocks.markdown:
A load balancer is a smart host at the door, spreading requests across a pool of servers.

- Clients talk to **one address** (a virtual IP or DNS name); the LB hides how many servers there really are.
- Add, remove, or restart servers without clients noticing.
- **Health checks** poke each server and pull the dead ones from rotation, so users never hit a dead box.
- It spreads load and survives failures — but it's a router, not a magic capacity multiplier.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for what
blocks.markdown:
Match the situation to the tool.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Raw speed, any protocol | L4 LB |
| URL routing, retries, WAF | L7 LB |
| Same key on same server | Consistent hashing |
| Uneven, long-lived connections | Least connections |

blocks.subTitle: Why it exists
blocks.markdown:
One server has a hard ceiling — fixed cores, RAM, and a network card that tops out.

- Past that, you **scale out** (more boxes), not up — there's no infinitely large server.
- The instant you have many servers, you need one stable front address to fan requests out. That's the LB.
- **Servers fail constantly** at scale. With health checks in the middle, a dead box is a non-event, not an outage.
- See [capacity-estimation](capacity-estimation) for sizing the fleet.

blocks.subTitle: L4 vs L7
blocks.markdown:
The single most important distinction: which layer the LB reads.

![L4 versus L7 load balancing comparison](assets/load-balancing-proxies/l4-vs-l7.svg)

- **L4 (transport)** — sees only IP and port, forwards packets. Blazing fast, protocol-agnostic, but content-blind.
- **L7 (application)** — parses the HTTP request: path, headers, cookies. Routes `/api` vs `/images`, retries, runs a WAF, terminates TLS — at the cost of CPU and a little latency.
- L7 is a full proxy: it terminates the client connection and opens a fresh one to the backend.
- In AWS: **NLB is L4, ALB is L7**.

blocks.subTitle: Topology & health checks
blocks.markdown:
Clients hit one address; the LB owns a pool and only sends traffic to live members.

![Load balancer topology with health checks](assets/load-balancing-proxies/lb-topology.svg)

- **Active checks** probe each backend (TCP connect, or HTTP GET to `/healthz`) every few seconds.
- Typical config: check every 5s, unhealthy after **3** fails, healthy after **2** passes — the thresholds (hysteresis) stop a flapping box from churning.
- **Passive checks** just watch real traffic — free, but only notice once users hit the bad server.

assets.alt: Load balancer topology with health checks

blocks.subTitle: The four algorithms
blocks.markdown:
How the LB picks the next server — a classic interview list.

- **Round robin** — fixed rotation 1, 2, 3, 1… Fair when servers and requests are identical; ignores how busy each box is.
- **Weighted round robin** — bigger servers get proportionally more. Use for a **heterogeneous** fleet.
- **Least connections** — send to the box with the fewest active connections. Wins for **long-lived or uneven** work (websockets, streaming).
- **Consistent hashing** — `hash(key) → server` so the same key sticks; only ~1/N keys remap when the pool changes.

blocks.subTitle: Consistent hashing math
blocks.markdown:
Plain modulo breaks the moment the server count changes.

```python
server = hash(user_id) % N   # N -> N+1 remaps ~every key
```

Consistent hashing puts servers on a ring; a key walks clockwise to the next server point.

- Add a server and only the keys in its new arc move — about **1/N**, not all of them.
- **Virtual nodes** (many ring points per server) smooth the distribution.
- This is why every distributed cache and partitioner uses it ([caching](caching)).

blocks.subTitle: Reverse vs forward proxy
blocks.markdown:
A load balancer is one kind of reverse proxy — same machinery, opposite direction.

![Reverse proxy versus forward proxy](assets/load-balancing-proxies/reverse-vs-forward-proxy.svg)

- **Reverse proxy** sits in front of *your servers*, representing them to the world — balances, terminates TLS, hides topology.
- **Forward proxy** sits in front of *clients*, representing them to the internet — egress control, filtering, anonymity, client caching.

blocks.subTitle: What you actually trade on
blocks.markdown:
Every LB decision is one of these tensions.

| Trade | Pick by |
|---|---|
| Speed vs intelligence | L4 fast, L7 HTTP-aware |
| Even load vs stickiness | Round robin vs consistent hash |
| Central TLS vs end-to-end | Terminate vs re-encrypt |

- Identical servers → round robin; different sizes → weighted.
- If any server can serve anything → least connections; if a key must stick → consistent hashing.

blocks.subTitle: Stateless beats sticky
blocks.markdown:
Sticky sessions pin a user to one backend (cookie or IP hash) so its in-memory state stays reachable.

- The cost is real: hot spots from heavy users, and **lost sessions** when that box dies.
- The better fix: make servers **stateless**, storing sessions in a shared store like Redis ([caching](caching)).
- Then any server serves any user — load balancing, scaling, and failover all get trivial.
- Reach for stickiness as a stopgap, never a design goal.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The same role, many implementations.

- **HAProxy** — battle-tested software LB, laser-focused on fast, stable L4/L7 balancing.
- **nginx** — solved the C10k problem as a web server, then became the Swiss-army reverse proxy and L7 LB.
- **Envoy** — sidecar L7 proxy for service meshes; dynamic xDS config and deep observability, powers Istio.
- **AWS** — NLB (L4, source-IP-preserving, millions of req/s) vs ALB (L7, path/host routing, websockets, WAF).

blocks.subTitle: HA, deploys & monitoring
blocks.markdown:
The LB itself is a single point of failure — never run just one.

- **HA**: redundant LBs in active-passive (floating IP via VRRP/keepalived) or active-active; globally, DNS plus **anycast** route clients to the nearest healthy site.
- **Deploys**: **connection draining** stops new requests but lets in-flight ones finish before shutdown.
- **Monitor**: healthy-host count, per-backend distribution, p99 latency, and **5xx codes** — 502/503 often means no healthy backend, 504 means backends timing out.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"The LB makes my app scale."** It spreads load; it doesn't create capacity. Saturated backends just share the pain.
- **"Round robin gives even load."** It evens request *count*, not *work* — uneven costs need least connections.
- **"`hash % N` is fine for sharding."** Only if N never changes; otherwise nearly all keys remap. Use consistent hashing.
- **"My health check returns 200, so I'm covered."** A shallow check keeps a broken box in; a too-deep one tied to a shared DB ejects the whole fleet at once.
- **"TLS terminated means fully encrypted."** Only client→LB is; LB→backend is plaintext unless re-encrypted.
